extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, policymakers, and researchers seeking an overview of the Affordable Care Act's provisions and requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes statutory provisions, eligibility rules, program criteria, and regulatory requirements established by the U.S. Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA). Useful for understanding who is covered, what benefits and protections are required, program mechanics, and state/federal implementation choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranteed issue
rubrics_metrics.description: All new individual major medical health insurance policies sold to individuals and families faced new requirements. Guaranteed issue prohibits insurers from denying coverage to individuals because of preexisting conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States were required to ensure availability of insurance for individual children who did not have coverage via their families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial community rating
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial community rating allows premiums to vary only by age and location, regardless of preexisting conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premiums for older applicants can be no more than three times those for the youngest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential health benefits requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential health benefits must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The National Academy of Medicine defines these to include ambulatory patient services; emergency services; hospitalization; maternity and newborn care; mental health and substance use disorder services; prescription drugs; rehabilitative and habilitative services and devices; laboratory services; preventive and wellness services and chronic disease management; and pediatric services, including oral and vision care. In determining essential benefits, the law required that standard benefits should offer at least that of a 'typical employer plan'. States may require additional services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive care and women's services coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventive care and screenings for women—'[A]ll Food and Drug Administration approved contraceptive methods, sterilization procedures, and patient education and counseling for all women with reproductive capacity'—must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mandate applies to all employers and educational institutions except for religious organizations. Preventive care, vaccinations and medical screenings cannot be subject to copayments, coinsurance or deductibles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on annual and lifetime coverage caps
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual and lifetime coverage caps on essential benefits were banned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on rescission (dropping policyholders when ill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurers are forbidden from dropping policyholders when they become ill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum out-of-pocket (MOOP) cap requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All policies must provide an annual maximum out-of-pocket payment cap for an individual's or family's medical expenses (excluding premiums). After the MOOP payment is reached, all remaining costs must be paid by the insurer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage tiers and actuarial values (bronze/silver/gold/platinum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law established four tiers of coverage: bronze, silver, gold and platinum. All categories offer essential health benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories vary in their division of premiums and out-of-pocket costs. The percentages of health care costs that plans are expected to cover on average are: 60% (bronze), 70% (silver), 80% (gold), and 90% (platinum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals process for coverage determinations and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurers are required to implement an appeals process for coverage determination and claims on all new plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurers must spend at least 80–85% of premium dollars on health costs; rebates must be issued if this is violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required percentage varies (80–85%) depending on market segment; rebates are issued to enrollees when the insurer fails to meet the MLR standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual mandate (requirement to have insurance or pay penalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual mandate required everyone to have insurance or pay a penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mandate and limits on open enrollment were designed to avoid adverse selection and the 'insurance death spiral'. Note: the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 set the penalty at $0 starting in 2019.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of exemptions from individual mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain groups were exempt from the individual mandate (e.g., undocumented immigrants; Medicaid-eligible citizens not enrolled in Medicaid; citizens whose insurance would cost more than 8% of household income; citizens who live in states that opt out of Medicaid expansion and who qualify for neither existing Medicaid coverage nor subsidized coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Health insurance exchanges requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: ACA mandated that health insurance exchanges be provided for each state; exchanges are regulated, largely online marketplaces, administered by either federal or state governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that set up their own exchanges have discretion on standards and prices, can approve plans for sale and impose additional coverage requirements (e.g., abortion). Alternatively, states can let the federal government operate their exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premium subsidies eligibility and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals with household incomes between 100% and 400% of the federal poverty level (FPL) are eligible to receive federal subsidies for premiums for policies purchased on an ACA exchange, subject to eligibility rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility excludes those eligible for Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, or other forms of public assistance, and those with access to affordable employer coverage. Married people must file taxes jointly to receive subsidies. Subsidies stop at 400% FPL. Subsidies are provided as an advanceable, refundable tax credit and are calculated to reduce the premium for the second-lowest-cost silver plan (SLCSP) to a sliding-scale percentage of income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-sharing reduction (CSR) subsidies
rubrics_metrics.description: ACA mandated that insurers reduce copayments and deductibles for ACA exchange enrollees earning less than 250% of the FPL, funded by cost-sharing reduction subsidies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CSR payments were to be paid to insurance companies to fund the reductions. CSR payments were treated differently in budgetary terms (not explicitly defined as mandatory), which led to litigation and disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-corridor program (temporary risk management)
rubrics_metrics.description: The risk-corridor program was a temporary risk management device (intended 2014–2016) where DHHS would cover some losses for insurers whose plans performed worse than expected; profit-making insurers would help pay loss-making insurers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program intended to encourage insurers into the exchange market. Program did not pay for itself as planned; funding and appropriations restrictions led to litigation and disputes over payment obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinsurance program (temporary premium stabilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A temporary reinsurance program (2014–2016) was meant to stabilize premiums by reducing the incentive for insurers to raise premiums due to concerns about higher-risk enrollees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinsurance was based on retrospective costs rather than prospective risk evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk adjustment (permanent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk adjustment involves transferring funds from plans with lower-risk enrollees to plans with higher-risk enrollees to encourage competition on value rather than by attracting healthier enrollees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of the three risk-management programs (risk corridors, reinsurance, risk adjustment), only risk adjustment was permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicaid expansion criteria and federal funding schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: ACA revised and expanded Medicaid eligibility starting in 2014: U.S. citizens and legal residents with income up to 133% of the poverty line would qualify in participating states. The federal government would pay 100% of the increased cost in 2014–2016; then taper to 90% in 2020 and subsequent years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 5% 'income disregard' made the effective eligibility limit 138% of the poverty level. The Supreme Court ruled states could opt out of the Medicaid expansion without losing existing federal Medicaid funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicare payment and savings reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicare reimbursements were reduced to insurers and drug companies for private Medicare Advantage policies and to hospitals that failed standards of efficiency and care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These were intended to reduce excessive payments and generate savings within Medicare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Medicare-related taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Income from self-employment and wages above specified thresholds are subject to an additional Medicare tax of 0.9%; a 3.8% tax was applied to net investment income for those above income thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds: $200,000 for single, $250,000 for married filing jointly (with a different threshold for married filing separately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excise taxes on high-cost plans and specific industries
rubrics_metrics.description: ACA included an excise tax of 40% ('Cadillac tax') on total employer premium spending in excess of specified dollar amounts (indexed to inflation). It also included excise taxes on importers and manufacturers of prescription drugs, a 2.3% excise tax on medical devices, and a 10% excise tax on indoor tanning services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cadillac tax was delayed multiple times and ultimately repealed as part of later legislation; other excise taxes were also subject to later repeal or modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: SCHIP (CHIP) enrollment simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: The State Children's Health Insurance Program enrollment process was simplified under ACA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent coverage to age 26
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependents may remain on their parents' insurance plan until their 26th birthday, including dependents who no longer live with their parents, are not a dependent on a parent's tax return, are no longer a student, or are married.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision took effect September 23, 2010.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer mandate (employer shared responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Businesses that employ fifty or more people but do not offer health insurance to their full-time employees are assessed additional tax if the government has subsidized a full-time employee's healthcare through tax deductions or other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was included to encourage employers to continue providing insurance once exchanges began operating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery system reforms to constrain costs and improve quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act includes delivery system reforms such as Medicare payment changes to discourage hospital-acquired conditions and readmissions, bundled payment initiatives, the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation, the Independent Payment Advisory Board, and accountable care organizations (ACOs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reforms are intended to prioritize quality and care coordination over volume of services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospital quality incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Health care cost/quality initiatives included incentives to reduce hospital infections, adopt electronic medical records, coordinate care and prioritize quality over quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bundled payments requirement (episode-based payments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicare switched from fee-for-service to bundled payments for certain episodes of care — a single payment to a hospital and physician group for a defined episode (e.g., hip replacement) rather than separate payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountable Care Organizations (ACO) participation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: ACOs are groups of providers that commit to coordinated care for Medicare patients; they can receive bonus payments for minimizing costs while achieving quality benchmarks and are subject to penalties for missing benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike HMOs, ACO patients are not required to obtain all care from the ACO. ACOs must achieve quality-of-care goals to receive shared savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicare Part D 'doughnut hole' discounts and phase-out
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicare Part D participants received a 50% discount on brand-name drugs purchased after exhausting their initial coverage and before reaching the catastrophic-coverage threshold; the 'doughnut hole' was to be completely filled by 2020.

rubrics_metrics.name: State innovation waivers (1115/1332-style criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: From 2017 onwards, states can apply for a 'waiver for state innovation' allowing experiments that meet certain criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain a waiver, a state must pass legislation setting up an alternative health system that provides insurance at least as comprehensive and as affordable as ACA, covers at least as many residents and does not increase the federal deficit. These waivers can escape some central requirements (including the individual and employer mandates and the provision of an insurance exchange); the state would receive compensation equal to the aggregate amount of federal subsidies and tax credits for which its residents and employers would have been eligible under ACA if they cannot be paid under the state plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer-operated and oriented plans (CO-OP) and federal loan support
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer Operated and Oriented Plans (CO-OP), member-governed non-profit insurers, could start providing health care coverage based on a 5-year federal loan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of 2017, only a small number of the original CO-OPs remained in operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLASS Act (long-term care insurance) — establishment and repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Community Living Assistance Services and Supports Act (CLASS Act) established a voluntary public long-term care insurance option for employees; the program was abolished as impractical without ever having taken effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nutrition labeling requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Nutrition labeling requirements were included in ACA and officially took effect in 2010 but implementation was delayed; they took effect on May 7, 2018.
